steps.label: The mole
lines: One mole is the amount of substance that

steps.why: The mole is defined by a counting standard: the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. Naming the particles and the standard makes the definition complete.
common_mistakes: Defining the mole as 'the molecular weight in grams'. That is a consequence, not the definition.
Leaving out carbon-12 and its 12 g.
steps.memory_tip: The definition has two anchors: 12 g and carbon-12.
steps.margin_note: Atoms, molecules or ions — say which particles are being counted.

steps.label: Avogadro's number
lines: It is the number of elementary particles
present in one mole of any substance.
steps.why: Avogadro's number is the count fixed by the mole definition, and every mole of any substance holds exactly this many particles.
common_mistakes: Writing 6.022 × 10²² or another wrong power of ten.
steps.memory_tip: 6.022 multiplied by 10²³, and 10²³ is 1 followed by 23 zeros — the power 23 is the part to protect.
steps.margin_note: Box the value with its unit mol⁻¹.

insider_note: Two questions, one mark each, and the second is a number that must be exactly right, power of ten and mol⁻¹ included. The mole definition needs the carbon-12 standard, not the molecular-weight shortcut.
